items.title: Harold Danko interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 28, 2021
items.q: the one that I got originally was Antal Dorati, the Minneapolis Symphony.

ctx.x: You know when — I’ve had the experience of hearing “The Rite of Spring” live twice and both times I felt like I’d been either run through a washing machine and hung up to dry, and all these like, and so I was really surprised to come across from his 1936 autobiography and I’m paraphrasing a little bit here but he said, “I consider that music is by its very nature essentially powerless to express anything at all. Expression has never been an inherent property of music.” I go really? © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

Pretty wild. I remember reading that a long time ago. And, okay. It’s the way he — I mean I think it’s like, he’s like, at that point you know he’s friends with Ravel, he’s friends with Debussy. A lot of those kind of harmonies are present in Debussy a little less functional and Ravel almost functional. But Stravinsky puts the rhythmic element on it and kind of, I forget, you know he isolates these sounds away from a context of harmony. And I think that’s like, you know rather than being totally atonal, when I…
Yeah. It’s fascinating to think that the dance was the, I guess impetus for the music, but now the music does it all.
